overview.core_concept: The Read-Eval-Print Loop establishes an interactive command-line interface by continuously displaying a prompt, reading user input, and gracefully handling termination.
overview.overview:
When you open a terminal, you are interacting with one of the oldest and most powerful user interfaces in computer science: the shell. At its heart, a shell is simply a program waiting patiently for your instructions, executing them, and showing you the results. This continuous interaction relies on a foundational software pattern known as the Read-Eval-Print Loop, or REPL.

Building your own shell from scratch allows you to look behind the curtain of operating system interactions. Instead of relying on abstract graphical environments, you will learn how text flows from standard input, how programs process lines of commands, and how control flow manages application lifecycles. By breaking down the shell into manageable steps—starting with a simple prompt, moving to reading input, and concluding with a clean exit mechanism—you will master the core mechanics that power every modern command-line environment.

sections.title: Display Shell Prompt
sections.content: A shell prompt is a visual indicator that signals the system is ready to accept user commands. Much like a host welcoming a guest at a door, the prompt communicates state, readiness, and context. Mechanically, printing a prompt involves writing a string directly to standard output without appending an automatic newline, ensuring the user types their command immediately adjacent to the indicator. Without a prompt, an interactive program would leave the user staring at a blank screen, unable to discern whether the program is frozen, processing in the background, or waiting for input. Designing an effective prompt establishes the primary communication channel between the human operator and the underlying system loop.

sections.title: Read User Input
sections.content: Once the prompt is displayed, the program must pause execution and listen for user input from standard input streams. Reading user input interactively requires buffered processing because humans type at variable speeds and input arrives character by character. The system collects these characters into a memory buffer until it detects a delimiter, typically a newline character generated when the user presses the enter key. This buffered stream is then parsed into a usable string format for the application logic. Handling input streams correctly also involves managing potential errors, such as unexpected stream closures or read failures, ensuring the application remains robust under various operating conditions.

sections.title: Handle Exit Command
sections.content: An interactive loop cannot run indefinitely without a reliable escape hatch. Graceful termination is critical for releasing system resources, flushing output buffers, and returning control to the parent process or operating system shell. Handling an exit involves monitoring incoming input for specific sentinel values or command strings that signify termination intent, as well as recognizing end-of-file signals generated by keyboard shortcuts. When a termination condition is met, the application performs necessary cleanup operations and exits cleanly with an appropriate status code, preventing hanging processes and orphaned resource allocations.

sections.title: Tokenize Input String
sections.content: Tokenization is the foundational process of breaking a continuous stream of characters into smaller, meaningful elements known as tokens. Imagine a conveyor belt moving raw text items past a scanner; when the scanner detects a specific boundary character, such as a space or a newline, it marks the end of one item and the beginning of the next. In systems programming, this boundary is typically any whitespace character. Without tokenization, an entire command line would be treated as a single massive file path or command name, rendering execution impossible. The parser reads through the input character by character or word by word, accumulating non-whitespace characters into a growing buffer until a separator is encountered. Once the separator is hit, the accumulated buffer is emitted as a complete token, and the parser resets to capture the next segment. This simple yet powerful mechanism transforms unstructured user input into a slice of distinct command arguments ready for downstream processing.

sections.title: Handle Quoted Arguments
sections.content: While simple whitespace splitting works for basic commands, real-world usage frequently requires passing arguments that contain spaces themselves, such as file paths with spaces or multi-word search queries. To solve this, parsers introduce stateful scanning through the use of quotation marks. Think of quotes as toggle switches for the parser rules. When the parser encounters an opening quote, it enters a specialized state where whitespace delimiters are temporarily ignored. Instead of treating a space as a boundary, the parser accumulates spaces inside the token buffer until a matching closing quote is encountered. This state machine approach ensures that characters like spaces, which normally separate tokens, are treated as literal data when enclosed within quotes. Implementing this requires tracking whether the parser is currently inside a quoted region, ensuring that malformed quotes or nested scenarios are handled gracefully according to defined syntax rules.

sections.title: Spawn Child Process
sections.content: When a user types an external command into a shell, the shell cannot execute it directly inside its own memory space without risking its own stability. Instead, the shell requests the operating system kernel to fork a new process or spawn a fresh child execution context. Think of the shell as a manager delegating a specialized task to a contractor. The manager provides the name of the tool to run along with a list of arguments, and the operating system locates the binary on disk, allocates memory, sets up file descriptors, and begins execution. Passing arguments correctly ensures the binary receives the exact flags and parameters intended by the user.

sections.title: Wait for Process Completion
sections.content: Once a child process is spawned, the parent shell faces a choice: run concurrently or wait. For a standard interactive shell, the user expects to see the prompt return only after the running program has finished its work. This requires blocking the parent process until the operating system signals that the child has terminated. Think of this like a conductor waiting for an orchestra to finish playing a movement before cueing the next piece. The operating system handles the synchronization, allowing the shell to pause its main loop, collect the exit status when the child exits, and restore prompt readiness.

sections.title: Handle Execution Errors
sections.content: In a robust environment, things inevitably go wrong. A user might misspell a command name, reference a non-existent binary, or attempt to run a program without proper permissions. If a shell panics or crashes when encountering such failures, the user experience breaks down completely. Graceful error handling ensures that when the operating system fails to locate a binary or rejects execution, the shell captures the error, reports a meaningful diagnostic message to standard error, and returns control to the prompt. This resilience separates fragile prototypes from production-grade tools.

Such operations require native handling inside the core process logic.

sections.title: Implement CD Command
sections.content: The working directory is a fundamental property of any running process, inherited by all children spawned from it. When a user requests to change directories, altering a spawned subprocess changes only that temporary child's path, leaving the parent shell stranded in the original folder. To achieve persistent navigation, the shell process must invoke system-level path resolution routines internally. Think of the shell as a captain steering a ship; if the captain tells a crew member to walk to a different room on a separate vessel, the captain's own ship does not move. The captain must walk through the compartments directly. Similarly, directory modification is an introspective operation that must update the working state of the main execution context. Handling path arguments securely, managing relative versus absolute paths, and handling potential permission or existence errors form the core of robust directory navigation within a process.

sections.title: Dispatch Built-ins
sections.content: As a command parser receives user input, it faces a fork in the road: should the instruction trigger an external executable located on the file system, or should it invoke a routine baked directly into the shell binary? Command dispatching acts as a traffic controller at this intersection. Before searching system paths or spawning child processes, the execution engine inspects the command name against a registry of known internal keywords. If a match occurs, control flows straight to the corresponding internal handler function. Imagine a restaurant where most orders require sending a ticket to the kitchen, but certain quick requests are handled immediately at the counter by the cashier. Dispatching lets the shell identify those counter-service commands instantly, saving system overhead, avoiding process creation latency, and preserving access to internal memory structures.

overview.core_concept: Input and output redirection allows a command-line shell to intercept standard streams and reroute them to or from files instead of the interactive terminal.
overview.overview:
Up to this point, every command executed in the custom shell has communicated with the user through standard input via the keyboard and standard output via the terminal screen. While interactive communication is essential, operating systems gain immense power through composition and data persistence. In this milestone, the shell unlocks file redirection, allowing users to save command outputs to disk or feed file contents directly into programs as inputs.

Imagine plumbing in a house: by default, faucets empty into drains. Redirection introduces flexible hoses and adapters that route water into storage tanks or feed it from external reservoirs instead. Understanding how to parse redirection symbols and reassign standard operating system streams gives the shell true pipeline capability, bridging interactive command entry with robust file management.

sections.title: Parse Redirection Operators
sections.content:
When a command string is typed into the shell, it arrives as a continuous stream of text that must be tokenized into discrete arguments. Certain tokens carry special meaning: symbols like the greater-than sign indicate output redirection, while the less-than sign indicates input redirection. Parsing redirection operators involves scanning the tokenized argument list to identify these special symbols and extracting the target filename that immediately follows them.

Think of this phase as a postal sorting facility inspecting address labels. The sorter separates regular cargo from routing instructions. When a redirection operator is encountered, it and its target file are separated from the main command arguments so that the execution engine does not accidentally pass the redirection symbols as regular command-line flags to the underlying program. Building a robust parser ensures that operators are correctly identified, edge cases like missing target files are caught early, and the remaining command arguments stay pristine for execution.

sections.title: Apply File Redirection
sections.content:
Once redirection operators and their target files are successfully identified, the shell must configure the standard input and output streams before executing the target program. Operating systems represent open files and communication channels as integer descriptors, with standard input, standard output, and standard error occupying well-known initial slots. Applying redirection involves opening the specified file on disk and swapping the standard stream descriptors to point to the new file resource.

Imagine redirecting an actor's microphone feed during a live stage play. Before the scene begins, the sound engineer reroutes the input source or the speaker output behind the scenes without the audience needing to change how they listen. In the same way, the process itself remains completely unaware that its output is flowing into a file rather than the terminal screen, because the operating system kernel handles the underlying descriptor redirection transparently at the process startup boundary.

levels.title: Wait for Process Completion
levels.goal: Block the shell until the spawned child process finishes execution.

narrative.hook: Previously, our shell could successfully launch external commands as child processes, but it immediately raced ahead without waiting for them to finish.
